issues.topic: "Your $1,299 order is confirmed" emails with a number to call
issues.subject: Scam alert: "Your $1,299 order is confirmed" emails with a number to call
issues.preheader: Don't call the number in the email. Check your orders in the store's own app.
issues.headline: "Your $1,299 order is confirmed" emails with a number to call
issues.example: "Order #A-77812 confirmed: MacBook Pro, $1,299.00. Not you? Call our fraud desk within 24 hours at 1-555-0142 to cancel and get a refund."
explain: It arrives by email, usually from a big online store or payment app. A big purchase you never made, sent to scare you into acting fast.
A phone number to call, instead of "check your account". A deadline to cancel. On the call, they'll want remote access to your computer or your bank login "to refund you".
issues.tell: Don't call the number in the email. Check your orders in the store's own app.
steps: Don't call the number in the email. Open the store's app or type its website yourself and check your orders.
No order there? Delete the email. It's fake.
**Called and let them onto your computer?** Disconnect it from the internet, call your bank on the number on your card, and change your passwords from another device.
quick_hits: **Gift cards drained before you even give them:** A scratched, peeled or re-stuck PIN strip on the back. Check the package and the PIN area before you pay. Pick one from the back of the rack.
**Marketplace "buyers" who ask for a code to prove you're real:** The buyer wants to "verify" you before they've even seen the item. Never share a code someone sends you, with anyone.
**A family member's voice, crying for money:** It's urgent and secret: don't tell anyone else in the family. Hang up and call the family member on the number you already have for them.

**"Rate products from home, earn $800 a week" job texts:** A recruiter you never contacted texts out of the blue. Don't reply. Real employers don't recruit by surprise text and never ask you to pay to work.
issues.job: Tell one person who'd get a email like this about it. The rule to pass on: Don't call the number in the email. Open the store's app or type its website yourself and check your orders.

issues.subject: Scam alert: "Your package is on hold" texts are spiking before Black Friday
issues.preheader: A $1.99 redelivery fee is how they get your card. Track packages in the shipper's app instead.
issues.headline: "Your package is on hold" texts are spiking before Black Friday
issues.example: "USPS: Your package is on hold due to an incomplete address. Update within 12 hours and pay a $1.99 redelivery fee: usps-redeliver-help.com"
explain: It arrives by text, usually from a delivery company, from a number you don't know. A text you didn't sign up for, from a regular phone number, about a package you can't name.
A tiny fee and a short deadline. The fee is the bait; the page wants your full card details. A link that only looks like the shipper's site. The real domain is right before the first single slash.
issues.tell: A $1.99 redelivery fee is how they get your card. Track packages in the shipper's app instead.
steps: Don't tap. Track packages in the shipper's app or by typing its website yourself.
Expecting something? Check the order page on the store's own site or app.
**Typed your card number?** Call the number on the back of your card and ask for a new one. Then watch your statement for small test charges.
quick_hits: **Black Friday ads for shops that don't exist:** Prices far below what anyone else charges. Search the shop's name with "scam", "review" or "complaints" before you buy.
**Fake charities ahead of Giving Tuesday:** It thanks you for a donation you don't remember making. Look the charity up before you give: search its name plus "complaint", "review" or "scam".
**The loud "your computer is infected" pop-up:** It's loud, scary and won't close. Don't call. Close the browser; if it won't close, restart the computer.

**"Your personal info is for sale on the dark web" emails:** A scary claim from a company you never signed up with. Don't click. If you're worried, change passwords on the sites you use and turn on two-step sign-in.

explain: It arrives by call, usually from a grandchild, then a "lawyer". A family emergency, then a "lawyer" or "officer".
A courier sent to your door for cash. Secrecy.

steps: Hang up and call your grandchild or their parents.
Never hand cash to a courier.
**Already paid?** Call your bank and local police right away, then the Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-372-8311.
quick_hits: **Ghost preparers who won't sign your return:** They won't sign the return or give a PTIN. Use a preparer who signs and has a PTIN.
**Investment "clubs" in group chats with a professor and big wins:** Huge returns and screenshots from other "members". Don't download their app or send money.
**Fake IRS letters with a QR code to "claim your refund":** A refund you didn't expect, with a deadline. Don't scan it.
**"A return was already filed with your SSN":** Your e-file is rejected because your SSN was already used. Follow the IRS identity theft guide on irs.gov.

issues.preheader: Nobody real charges you upfront to get your money back. This is the second scam.
issues.headline: Recovery offices that will get your scam losses back, for a fee
issues.example: "This is the Federal Fraud Recovery Unit. We located $8,400 you lost last year. A $350 processing fee by gift card releases the refund today."
explain: It arrives by call or email, usually from a "fraud recovery" office, a law firm or a government agency. They know you lost money before, and offer to get it back.
The refund needs a fee first: processing, retainer or tax. They want gift cards, crypto or a wire.
issues.tell: Nobody real charges you upfront to get your money back. This is the second scam.
steps: Hang up. Look up the agency or firm's number yourself and call it.
Never pay upfront for a refund, or give account numbers to "deposit" one.
**Paid already?** Call the gift card company or your bank on the number on the card right away and ask them to stop or reverse it.
quick_hits: **Calls from "the FTC" about a prize, a virus or your account:** The caller uses the FTC's name, sometimes a real employee's. Hang up. The FTC never calls to demand money.
**Free trials that only cost shipping, then charge every month:** "Free" still needs your card, for shipping or a fee. Find the terms and the cancel steps before you sign up. No terms, no order.
**Debt collectors who threaten arrest and won't give an address:** A debt you don't recognize. Ask for the collector's name, address and the creditor, in writing. Pay nothing yet.
**Credit repair that wants $499 up front to wipe your record:** They promise to remove true, accurate information.
